https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy8z.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The Gravelines nuclear power plant is cooled from a canal connected to the North Sea By Alys Davies Published 27 August 2026 A massive influx of jellyfish has led to the partial shutdown of a nuclear reactor in northern France. Two of Gravelines nuclear power station's six units were shut down on Wednesday and Thursday because of the presence of jellyfish in the seawater filtration system, which is used for cooling, ÃlectricitÃ© de France (EDF) said. A third unit has been shut down since 10 August due to the same issue, while a fourth has been closed for an inspection. Gravelines, one of the country's biggest nuclear power stations located between Dunkirk and Calais in the Hauts-de-France region, was also closed last August because of jellyfish in its filters. EDF said that units three, four and six were now shut. Unit three had only been reconnected to the grid on 18 August after the first wave of jellyfish earlier this month, the company said, while units one and two were also operating at reduced power as a preventative measure. Gravelines' six units each produce 900 megawatts of power. The station is cooled from a canal connected to the North Sea. Several species of jellyfish are native and can be seen around the coast when the waters are warm. Jellyfish are at their most active in the warmer months. Hot weather increases plankton levels at the water's surface, drawing jellyfish up, experts say. Measures have been implemented to try to prevent jellyfish infiltration, including a partnership with fishermen who capture and release them further offshore, according to French outlet Ici. There have been similar issues at other nuclear stations, including at the Torness plant in Scotland in 2011 and Sweden's Oskarshamn plant in 2013, but such cases are rare. https://www.politico.eu/article/france-i.text: PARIS — France will increase its defense budget next year despite increasingly strained public finances, according to a document obtained by POLITICO. The French government will present later on Thursday a 2027 budget that earmarks €63.4 billion for military expenditures, compared with €57 billion this year. About 12% will be dedicated to nuclear deterrence and 43% to the purchase and maintenance of military equipment. That's in line with increases foreseen by the military planning law adopted over the summer. Advertisement Advertisement "To ensure our sovereignty, the government plans to strengthen our military capabilities through additional orders for major equipment (surface-to-air defense systems, anti-drone systems, and artificial intelligence)," the document reads. This means France's defense budget will have doubled under French President Emmanuel Macron's two terms, which started in 2017. The defense ministry is one of the very few to benefit from a budget increase in 2027. The government has announced a deficit target of 5% of GDP for next year, and the freeze on most other ministerial budgets at their 2026 levels has been confirmed.

https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-ai-li.text: BRUSSELS — EU parliamentarians are digging in on calls to revive an artificial intelligence liability law after receiving support from an unexpected ally: Open AI’s Sam Altman. “If something goes wrong with our models during training, there's gonna be some version of that we need to be responsible for,” Altman said in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO released Monday. “There's gonna need to be a liability framework for companies.” This spotlight on liability has given influential members of the European Parliament a told-you-so moment after the EU last year scrapped plans to legislate on responsibility and compensation for harms caused by AI makers and agents. Advertisement Advertisement The proposal by the European Commission for an AI liability law was killed amid a deep effort in Brussels to deregulate and reduce the legislative burden on companies — with the Commission arguing at the time that the proposal had little chance of securing sufficient political support. German conservative lawmaker Axel Voss, who led on the proposal for the European Parliament, wants Brussels to put liability back on the agenda in light of Altman’s comments. “I welcome this overdue moment of honesty. For years, the tech industry has argued that liability would stifle innovation,” he said. "Now even the CEO of OpenAI admits: Without liability, there is no trust.” The law, first proposed in 2022, “would have closed exactly the gap Altman is now describing: responsibility before deployment, during training and testing,” Voss said. One way governments could reduce AI risks is to apply product liability law, assigning responsibility (and penalties) to the makers of the most advanced AI models to nudge their development toward a safety-first approach. As concerns over the pace of frontier AI development and the harm caused make the question of liability impossible to ignore — and as proposals for AI liability rules gain support around the world — proponents say the EU’s decision to scrap the proposal hasn't aged well. Advertisement Advertisement The Commission has defended its landmark AI Act in response to mounting incidents and fears, while leaving the door open to additional rules addressing liability. In response to questions by POLITICO last week, the EU’s tech chief Henna Virkkunen said she would look into potential “loopholes” in the current legislation, while reiterating the need to be “very careful” when crafting new rules. The Commission didn't respond to POLITICO's request to comment for this article. Not too late? Social democrat lawmaker Brando Benifei, who helped write the EU’s AI rulebook, on Tuesday called the withdrawal of the liability proposal “a serious mistake,” saying obligations emerging from the AI Act were originally meant to be complemented by the rules to hold the companies liable. “Frontier models and high-risk systems need strict liability,” he said. Together with Irish independent lawmaker Michael McNamara and Greens member Kim van Sparrentak, the senior lawmakers are actively calling on the EU to introduce an AI liability act “to fill the legislative gaps currently existing for these kinds of incidents, so no people or European businesses are left empty-handed against these big providers when they cause harm,” POLITICO previously reported . Advertisement Advertisement "We have an AI Act that regulates use, but we have no clear rules on who pays when a foundation model itself is flawed, biased or causes harm. This is not tenable,” Voss said. He said it's not too late for Brussels to take another U-turn. “If the builder of a model admits he should be liable, the legislator should not be less ambitious than the industry.” But one senior Parliament official involved in the liability law proposal said that for the Commission, “it would be admitting they made a big mistake.” “If there is a major AI accident, creating more and more momentum for [action], they will probably call it differently — maybe an ‘Agentic AI Act,’ or ‘Protecting our Citizens from AI Act’ or whatever in order to hide past mistakes and flawed observations,” the official said. As Brussels considers how to address new risks, the rest of the world will be watching. “Altman says there will need to be a liability framework for models like his, but most likely one with many exceptions,” said Artur Bogucki, director of research at the think tank CEPS. “The EU needs a direct, targeted AI liability instrument, narrow and procedural at its core,” including obligations to log and disclose evidence, he said. Eliza Gkritsi contributed to this report. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.siasat.com/body-of-telangana.text: Hyderabad: The mortal remains of Avilala Sudarshan Goud, a migrant worker from Telangana's Jagtial district killed in a Russian missile strike in Ukraine, are expected to reach Hyderabad in the early hours of Saturday, October 31, nearly two months after his death. Sudarshan, 42, of Hasnabad village in Jagtial Urban mandal, died on Tuesday, September 1. He had gone to Ukraine for work and was employed as a formworker for reinforced concrete products and structures with BKBM LLC. According to a press note issued on Monday, October 26, the permission needed to move the body was reportedly delayed by the investigation into the strike, for which a criminal case has been registered. The wait was also prolonged by the question of who would pay for the repatriation. A letter from the Telangana General Administration Department (GAD) states that an official of the Embassy of India in Ukraine asked the family to pay Rs 6 lakh towards the expenses. The government sent a fax to the embassy on September 7 and a reminder on October 9, asking it to waive the charge or meet it from the Indian Community Welfare Fund (ICWF). Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy had earlier sanctioned Rs 6 lakh for the repatriation after Sudarshan's wife, Bhargavi, approached the CM Pravasi Prajavani grievance forum in Hyderabad. Jagtial Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) Dr Makunuri Sanjay Kumar then asked the state government to take up the matter with the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) and the Indian Embassy in Kyiv. The press note says Minister Adluri Lakshman Kumar also made a representation. On Saturday, October 24, Ahmad Nadeem, Principal Secretary (Political) in the GAD, wrote to Indian Ambassador to Ukraine Anjani Kumar seeking early repatriation. The letter asks that the ICWF meet the cost if necessary. Mandha Bheem Reddy, vice chairman of the Telangana government's Non-Resident Indian (NRI) Advisory Committee, said the government acted promptly after Bhargavi sought help. Route home Because air travel in Ukrainian airspace remains restricted, the coffin will be taken by road from Ukraine to Poland, according to the press note. It will then be flown by KLM Royal Dutch Airlines from Warsaw to Amsterdam and on to Hyderabad. The air journey is scheduled to begin on Thursday, October 29. After the body arrives at Hyderabad Airport, arrangements will be made to take it to Hasnabad for the final rites.
